    \newcommand*\pandocbounded[1]{%
      \sbox\pandoc@box{#1}%
      % scaling factors for width and height
      \Gscale@div\@tempa\textheight{\dimexpr\ht\pandoc@box+\dp\pandoc@box\relax}%
      \Gscale@div\@tempb\linewidth{\wd\pandoc@box}%
      % select the smaller of both
      \ifdim\@tempb\p@<\@tempa\p@
        \let\@tempa\@tempb
      \fi
      % scaling accordingly (\@tempa < 1)
      \ifdim\@tempa\p@<\p@
        \scalebox{\@tempa}{\usebox\pandoc@box}%
      % scaling not needed, use as it is
      \else
        \usebox{\pandoc@box}%
      \fi
    }

    % For linebreaks inside Verbatim environment from package fancyvrb.
    \makeatletter
        \newbox\Wrappedcontinuationbox
        \newbox\Wrappedvisiblespacebox
        \newcommand*\Wrappedvisiblespace {\textcolor{red}{\textvisiblespace}}
        \newcommand*\Wrappedcontinuationsymbol {\textcolor{red}{\llap{\tiny$\m@th\hookrightarrow$}}}
        \newcommand*\Wrappedcontinuationindent {3ex }
        \newcommand*\Wrappedafterbreak {\kern\Wrappedcontinuationindent\copy\Wrappedcontinuationbox}
        % Take advantage of the already applied Pygments mark-up to insert
        % potential linebreaks for TeX processing.
        %        {, <, #, %, $, ' and ": go to next line.
        %        _, }, ^, &, >, - and ~: stay at end of broken line.
        % Use of \textquotesingle for straight quote.
        \newcommand*\Wrappedbreaksatspecials {%
            \def\PYGZus{\discretionary{\char`\_}{\Wrappedafterbreak}{\char`\_}}%
            \def\PYGZob{\discretionary{}{\Wrappedafterbreak\char`\{}{\char`\{}}%
            \def\PYGZcb{\discretionary{\char`\}}{\Wrappedafterbreak}{\char`\}}}%
            \def\PYGZca{\discretionary{\char`\^}{\Wrappedafterbreak}{\char`\^}}%
            \def\PYGZam{\discretionary{\char`\&}{\Wrappedafterbreak}{\char`\&}}%
            \def\PYGZlt{\discretionary{}{\Wrappedafterbreak\char`\<}{\char`\<}}%
            \def\PYGZgt{\discretionary{\char`\>}{\Wrappedafterbreak}{\char`\>}}%
            \def\PYGZsh{\discretionary{}{\Wrappedafterbreak\char`\#}{\char`\#}}%
            \def\PYGZpc{\discretionary{}{\Wrappedafterbreak\char`\%}{\char`\%}}%
            \def\PYGZdl{\discretionary{}{\Wrappedafterbreak\char`\$}{\char`\$}}%
            \def\PYGZhy{\discretionary{\char`\-}{\Wrappedafterbreak}{\char`\-}}%
            \def\PYGZsq{\discretionary{}{\Wrappedafterbreak\textquotesingle}{\textquotesingle}}%
            \def\PYGZdq{\discretionary{}{\Wrappedafterbreak\char`\"}{\char`\"}}%
            \def\PYGZti{\discretionary{\char`\~}{\Wrappedafterbreak}{\char`\~}}%
        }
        % Some characters . , ; ? ! / are not pygmentized.
        % This macro makes them "active" and they will insert potential linebreaks
        \newcommand*\Wrappedbreaksatpunct {%
            \lccode`\~`\.\lowercase{\def~}{\discretionary{\hbox{\char`\.}}{\Wrappedafterbreak}{\hbox{\char`\.}}}%
            \lccode`\~`\,\lowercase{\def~}{\discretionary{\hbox{\char`\,}}{\Wrappedafterbreak}{\hbox{\char`\,}}}%
            \lccode`\~`\;\lowercase{\def~}{\discretionary{\hbox{\char`\;}}{\Wrappedafterbreak}{\hbox{\char`\;}}}%
            \lccode`\~`\:\lowercase{\def~}{\discretionary{\hbox{\char`\:}}{\Wrappedafterbreak}{\hbox{\char`\:}}}%
            \lccode`\~`\?\lowercase{\def~}{\discretionary{\hbox{\char`\?}}{\Wrappedafterbreak}{\hbox{\char`\?}}}%
            \lccode`\~`\!\lowercase{\def~}{\discretionary{\hbox{\char`\!}}{\Wrappedafterbreak}{\hbox{\char`\!}}}%
            \lccode`\~`\/\lowercase{\def~}{\discretionary{\hbox{\char`\/}}{\Wrappedafterbreak}{\hbox{\char`\/}}}%
            \catcode`\.\active
            \catcode`\,\active
            \catcode`\;\active
            \catcode`\:\active
            \catcode`\?\active
            \catcode`\!\active
            \catcode`\/\active
            \lccode`\~`\~
        }
    \makeatother

    \let\OriginalVerbatim=\Verbatim
    \makeatletter
    \renewcommand{\Verbatim}[1][1]{%
        %\parskip\z@skip
        \sbox\Wrappedcontinuationbox {\Wrappedcontinuationsymbol}%
        \sbox\Wrappedvisiblespacebox {\FV@SetupFont\Wrappedvisiblespace}%
        \def\FancyVerbFormatLine ##1{\hsize\linewidth
            \vtop{\raggedright\hyphenpenalty\z@\exhyphenpenalty\z@
                \doublehyphendemerits\z@\finalhyphendemerits\z@
                \strut ##1\strut}%
        }%
        % If the linebreak is at a space, the latter will be displayed as visible
        % space at end of first line, and a continuation symbol starts next line.
        % Stretch/shrink are however usually zero for typewriter font.
        \def\FV@Space {%
            \nobreak\hskip\z@ plus\fontdimen3\font minus\fontdimen4\font
            \discretionary{\copy\Wrappedvisiblespacebox}{\Wrappedafterbreak}
            {\kern\fontdimen2\font}%
        }%

        % Allow breaks at special characters using \PYG... macros.
        \Wrappedbreaksatspecials
        % Breaks at punctuation characters . , ; ? ! and / need catcode=\active
        \OriginalVerbatim[#1,codes*=\Wrappedbreaksatpunct]%
    }

\section{Linear Models and Regularization
Methods}\label{linear-models-and-regularization-methods}}

    In this lab we implement many of the techniques discussed in this
chapter. We import some of our libraries at this top level.

    \hypertarget{subset-selection-methods}{%
\subsection{Subset Selection Methods}\label{subset-selection-methods}}

Here we implement methods that reduce the number of parameters in a
model by restricting the model to a subset of the input variables.

\hypertarget{forward-selection}{%
\subsubsection{Forward Selection}\label{forward-selection}}

We will apply the forward-selection approach to the \texttt{Hitters}
data. We wish to predict a baseball player's \texttt{Salary} on the
basis of various statistics associated with performance in the previous
year.

First of all, we note that the \texttt{Salary} variable is missing for
some of the players. The \texttt{np.isnan()} function can be used to
identify the missing observations. It returns an array of the same shape
as the input vector, with a \texttt{True} for any elements that are
missing, and a \texttt{False} for non-missing elements. The
\texttt{sum()} method can then be used to count all of the missing
elements.

    \begin{tcolorbox}[breakable, size=fbox, boxrule=1pt, pad at break*=1mm,colback=cellbackground, colframe=cellborder]
\prompt{In}{incolor}{3}{\boxspacing}
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PY{n}{Hitters} \PY{o}{=} \PY{n}{load\PYZus{}data}\PY{p}{(}\PY{l+s+s1}{\PYZsq{}}\PY{l+s+s1}{Hitters}\PY{l+s+s1}{\PYZsq{}}\PY{p}{)}
\PY{n}{np}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{isnan}\PY{p}{(}\PY{n}{Hitters}\PY{p}{[}\PY{l+s+s1}{\PYZsq{}}\PY{l+s+s1}{Salary}\PY{l+s+s1}{\PYZsq{}}\PY{p}{]}\PY{p}{)}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{sum}\PY{p}{(}\PY{p}{)}
\end{Verbatim}
\end{tcolorbox}

            \begin{tcolorbox}[breakable, size=fbox, boxrule=.5pt, pad at break*=1mm, opacityfill=0]
\prompt{Out}{outcolor}{3}{\boxspacing}
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
59
\end{Verbatim}
\end{tcolorbox}
        
    We see that \texttt{Salary} is missing for 59 players. The
\texttt{dropna()} method of data frames removes all of the rows that
have missing values in any variable (by default --- see
\texttt{Hitters.dropna?}).

    \begin{tcolorbox}[breakable, size=fbox, boxrule=1pt, pad at break*=1mm,colback=cellbackground, colframe=cellborder]
\prompt{In}{incolor}{4}{\boxspacing}
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PY{n}{Hitters} \PY{o}{=} \PY{n}{Hitters}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{dropna}\PY{p}{(}\PY{p}{)}\PY{p}{;}
\PY{n}{Hitters}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{shape}
\end{Verbatim}
\end{tcolorbox}

            \begin{tcolorbox}[breakable, size=fbox, boxrule=.5pt, pad at break*=1mm, opacityfill=0]
\prompt{Out}{outcolor}{4}{\boxspacing}
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
(263, 20)
\end{Verbatim}
\end{tcolorbox}
        
    We first choose the best model using forward selection based on \(C_p\)
(6.2). This score is not built in as a metric to \texttt{sklearn}. We
therefore define a function to compute it ourselves, and use it as a
scorer. By default, \texttt{sklearn} tries to maximize a score, hence
our scoring function computes the negative \(C_p\) statistic.

    \begin{tcolorbox}[breakable, size=fbox, boxrule=1pt, pad at break*=1mm,colback=cellbackground, colframe=cellborder]
\prompt{In}{incolor}{5}{\boxspacing}
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PY{k}{def}\PY{+w}{ }\PY{n+nf}{nCp}\PY{p}{(}\PY{n}{sigma2}\PY{p}{,} \PY{n}{estimator}\PY{p}{,} \PY{n}{X}\PY{p}{,} \PY{n}{Y}\PY{p}{)}\PY{p}{:}
    \PY{l+s+s2}{\PYZdq{}}\PY{l+s+s2}{Negative Cp statistic}\PY{l+s+s2}{\PYZdq{}}
    \PY{n}{n}\PY{p}{,} \PY{n}{p} \PY{o}{=} \PY{n}{X}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{shape}
    \PY{n}{Yhat} \PY{o}{=} \PY{n}{estimator}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{predict}\PY{p}{(}\PY{n}{X}\PY{p}{)}
    \PY{n}{RSS} \PY{o}{=} \PY{n}{np}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{sum}\PY{p}{(}\PY{p}{(}\PY{n}{Y} \PY{o}{\PYZhy{}} \PY{n}{Yhat}\PY{p}{)}\PY{o}{*}\PY{o}{*}\PY{l+m+mi}{2}\PY{p}{)}
    \PY{k}{return} \PY{o}{\PYZhy{}}\PY{p}{(}\PY{n}{RSS} \PY{o}{+} \PY{l+m+mi}{2} \PY{o}{*} \PY{n}{p} \PY{o}{*} \PY{n}{sigma2}\PY{p}{)} \PY{o}{/} \PY{n}{n} 
\end{Verbatim}
\end{tcolorbox}

    We need to estimate the residual variance \(\sigma^2\), which is the
first argument in our scoring function above. We will fit the biggest
model, using all the variables, and estimate \(\sigma^2\) based on its
MSE.

    \begin{tcolorbox}[breakable, size=fbox, boxrule=1pt, pad at break*=1mm,colback=cellbackground, colframe=cellborder]
\prompt{In}{incolor}{6}{\boxspacing}
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PY{n}{design} \PY{o}{=} \PY{n}{MS}\PY{p}{(}\PY{n}{Hitters}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{columns}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{drop}\PY{p}{(}\PY{l+s+s1}{\PYZsq{}}\PY{l+s+s1}{Salary}\PY{l+s+s1}{\PYZsq{}}\PY{p}{)}\PY{p}{)}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{fit}\PY{p}{(}\PY{n}{Hitters}\PY{p}{)}
\PY{n}{Y} \PY{o}{=} \PY{n}{np}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{array}\PY{p}{(}\PY{n}{Hitters}\PY{p}{[}\PY{l+s+s1}{\PYZsq{}}\PY{l+s+s1}{Salary}\PY{l+s+s1}{\PYZsq{}}\PY{p}{]}\PY{p}{)}
\PY{n}{X} \PY{o}{=} \PY{n}{design}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{transform}\PY{p}{(}\PY{n}{Hitters}\PY{p}{)}
\PY{n}{sigma2} \PY{o}{=} \PY{n}{OLS}\PY{p}{(}\PY{n}{Y}\PY{p}{,}\PY{n}{X}\PY{p}{)}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{fit}\PY{p}{(}\PY{p}{)}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{scale}
\end{Verbatim}
\end{tcolorbox}

    The function \texttt{sklearn\_selected()} expects a scorer with just
three arguments --- the last three in the definition of \texttt{nCp()}
above. We use the function \texttt{partial()} first seen in Section
5.3.3 to freeze the first argument with our estimate of \(\sigma^2\).

    \begin{tcolorbox}[breakable, size=fbox, boxrule=1pt, pad at break*=1mm,colback=cellbackground, colframe=cellborder]
\prompt{In}{incolor}{7}{\boxspacing}
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PY{n}{neg\PYZus{}Cp} \PY{o}{=} \PY{n}{partial}\PY{p}{(}\PY{n}{nCp}\PY{p}{,} \PY{n}{sigma2}\PY{p}{)}
\end{Verbatim}
\end{tcolorbox}

    We can now use \texttt{neg\_Cp()} as a scorer for model selection.

    Along with a score we need to specify the search strategy. This is done
through the object \texttt{Stepwise()} in the \texttt{ISLP.models}
package. The method \texttt{Stepwise.first\_peak()} runs forward
stepwise until any further additions to the model do not result in an
improvement in the evaluation score. Similarly, the method
\texttt{Stepwise.fixed\_steps()} runs a fixed number of steps of
stepwise search.

    \begin{tcolorbox}[breakable, size=fbox, boxrule=1pt, pad at break*=1mm,colback=cellbackground, colframe=cellborder]
\prompt{In}{incolor}{8}{\boxspacing}
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PY{n}{strategy} \PY{o}{=} \PY{n}{Stepwise}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{first\PYZus{}peak}\PY{p}{(}\PY{n}{design}\PY{p}{,}
                               \PY{n}{direction}\PY{o}{=}\PY{l+s+s1}{\PYZsq{}}\PY{l+s+s1}{forward}\PY{l+s+s1}{\PYZsq{}}\PY{p}{,}
                               \PY{n}{max\PYZus{}terms}\PY{o}{=}\PY{n+nb}{len}\PY{p}{(}\PY{n}{design}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{terms}\PY{p}{)}\PY{p}{)}
\end{Verbatim}
\end{tcolorbox}

    We now fit a linear regression model with \texttt{Salary} as outcome
using forward selection. To do so, we use the function
\texttt{sklearn\_selected()} from the \texttt{ISLP.models} package. This
takes a model from \texttt{statsmodels} along with a search strategy and
selects a model with its \texttt{fit} method. Without specifying a
\texttt{scoring} argument, the score defaults to MSE, and so all 19
variables will be selected.

    \begin{tcolorbox}[breakable, size=fbox, boxrule=1pt, pad at break*=1mm,colback=cellbackground, colframe=cellborder]
\prompt{In}{incolor}{9}{\boxspacing}
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PY{n}{hitters\PYZus{}MSE} \PY{o}{=} \PY{n}{sklearn\PYZus{}selected}\PY{p}{(}\PY{n}{OLS}\PY{p}{,}
                               \PY{n}{strategy}\PY{p}{)}
\PY{n}{hitters\PYZus{}MSE}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{fit}\PY{p}{(}\PY{n}{Hitters}\PY{p}{,} \PY{n}{Y}\PY{p}{)}
\PY{n}{hitters\PYZus{}MSE}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{selected\PYZus{}state\PYZus{}}
\end{Verbatim}
\end{tcolorbox}

            \begin{tcolorbox}[breakable, size=fbox, boxrule=.5pt, pad at break*=1mm, opacityfill=0]
\prompt{Out}{outcolor}{9}{\boxspacing}
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
('Assists',
 'AtBat',
 'CAtBat',
 'CHits',
 'CHmRun',
 'CRBI',
 'CRuns',
 'CWalks',
 'Division',
 'Errors',
 'Hits',
 'HmRun',
 'League',
 'NewLeague',
 'PutOuts',
 'RBI',
 'Runs',
 'Walks',
 'Years')
\end{Verbatim}
\end{tcolorbox}
        
    Using \texttt{neg\_Cp} results in a smaller model, as expected, with
just 10 variables selected.

    \begin{tcolorbox}[breakable, size=fbox, boxrule=1pt, pad at break*=1mm,colback=cellbackground, colframe=cellborder]
\prompt{In}{incolor}{10}{\boxspacing}
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PY{n}{hitters\PYZus{}Cp} \PY{o}{=} \PY{n}{sklearn\PYZus{}selected}\PY{p}{(}\PY{n}{OLS}\PY{p}{,}
                               \PY{n}{strategy}\PY{p}{,}
                               \PY{n}{scoring}\PY{o}{=}\PY{n}{neg\PYZus{}Cp}\PY{p}{)}
\PY{n}{hitters\PYZus{}Cp}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{fit}\PY{p}{(}\PY{n}{Hitters}\PY{p}{,} \PY{n}{Y}\PY{p}{)}
\PY{n}{hitters\PYZus{}Cp}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{selected\PYZus{}state\PYZus{}}
\end{Verbatim}
\end{tcolorbox}

            \begin{tcolorbox}[breakable, size=fbox, boxrule=.5pt, pad at break*=1mm, opacityfill=0]
\prompt{Out}{outcolor}{10}{\boxspacing}
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
('Assists',
 'AtBat',
 'CAtBat',
 'CRBI',
 'CRuns',
 'CWalks',
 'Division',
 'Hits',
 'PutOuts',
 'Walks')
\end{Verbatim}
\end{tcolorbox}
        
    \hypertarget{choosing-among-models-using-the-validation-set-approach-and-cross-validation}{%
\subsubsection{Choosing Among Models Using the Validation Set Approach
and
Cross-Validation}\label{choosing-among-models-using-the-validation-set-approach-and-cross-validation}}

As an alternative to using \(C_p\), we might try cross-validation to
select a model in forward selection. For this, we need a method that
stores the full path of models found in forward selection, and allows
predictions for each of these. This can be done with the
\texttt{sklearn\_selection\_path()} estimator from \texttt{ISLP.models}.
The function \texttt{cross\_val\_predict()} from \texttt{ISLP.models}
computes the cross-validated predictions for each of the models along
the path, which we can use to evaluate the cross-validated MSE along the
path.

    Here we define a strategy that fits the full forward selection path.
While there are various parameter choices for
\texttt{sklearn\_selection\_path()}, we use the defaults here, which
selects the model at each step based on the biggest reduction in RSS.

    \begin{tcolorbox}[breakable, size=fbox, boxrule=1pt, pad at break*=1mm,colback=cellbackground, colframe=cellborder]
\prompt{In}{incolor}{11}{\boxspacing}
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PY{n}{strategy} \PY{o}{=} \PY{n}{Stepwise}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{fixed\PYZus{}steps}\PY{p}{(}\PY{n}{design}\PY{p}{,}
                                \PY{n+nb}{len}\PY{p}{(}\PY{n}{design}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{terms}\PY{p}{)}\PY{p}{,}
                                \PY{n}{direction}\PY{o}{=}\PY{l+s+s1}{\PYZsq{}}\PY{l+s+s1}{forward}\PY{l+s+s1}{\PYZsq{}}\PY{p}{)}
\PY{n}{full\PYZus{}path} \PY{o}{=} \PY{n}{sklearn\PYZus{}selection\PYZus{}path}\PY{p}{(}\PY{n}{OLS}\PY{p}{,} \PY{n}{strategy}\PY{p}{)}
\end{Verbatim}
\end{tcolorbox}

    We now fit the full forward-selection path on the \texttt{Hitters} data
and compute the fitted values.

    \begin{tcolorbox}[breakable, size=fbox, boxrule=1pt, pad at break*=1mm,colback=cellbackground, colframe=cellborder]
\prompt{In}{incolor}{12}{\boxspacing}
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PY{n}{full\PYZus{}path}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{fit}\PY{p}{(}\PY{n}{Hitters}\PY{p}{,} \PY{n}{Y}\PY{p}{)}
\PY{n}{Yhat\PYZus{}in} \PY{o}{=} \PY{n}{full\PYZus{}path}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{predict}\PY{p}{(}\PY{n}{Hitters}\PY{p}{)}
\PY{n}{Yhat\PYZus{}in}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{shape}
\end{Verbatim}
\end{tcolorbox}

            \begin{tcolorbox}[breakable, size=fbox, boxrule=.5pt, pad at break*=1mm, opacityfill=0]
\prompt{Out}{outcolor}{12}{\boxspacing}
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
(263, 20)
\end{Verbatim}
\end{tcolorbox}
        
    This gives us an array of fitted values --- 20 steps in all, including
the fitted mean for the null model --- which we can use to evaluate
in-sample MSE. As expected, the in-sample MSE improves each step we
take, indicating we must use either the validation or cross-validation
approach to select the number of steps. We fix the y-axis to range from
50,000 to 250,000 to compare to the cross-validation and validation set
MSE below, as well as other methods such as ridge regression, lasso and
principal components regression.

    \begin{tcolorbox}[breakable, size=fbox, boxrule=1pt, pad at break*=1mm,colback=cellbackground, colframe=cellborder]
\prompt{In}{incolor}{13}{\boxspacing}
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PY{n}{mse\PYZus{}fig}\PY{p}{,} \PY{n}{ax} \PY{o}{=} \PY{n}{subplots}\PY{p}{(}\PY{n}{figsize}\PY{o}{=}\PY{p}{(}\PY{l+m+mi}{8}\PY{p}{,}\PY{l+m+mi}{8}\PY{p}{)}\PY{p}{)}
\PY{n}{insample\PYZus{}mse} \PY{o}{=} \PY{p}{(}\PY{p}{(}\PY{n}{Yhat\PYZus{}in} \PY{o}{\PYZhy{}} \PY{n}{Y}\PY{p}{[}\PY{p}{:}\PY{p}{,}\PY{k+kc}{None}\PY{p}{]}\PY{p}{)}\PY{o}{*}\PY{o}{*}\PY{l+m+mi}{2}\PY{p}{)}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{mean}\PY{p}{(}\PY{l+m+mi}{0}\PY{p}{)}
\PY{n}{n\PYZus{}steps} \PY{o}{=} \PY{n}{insample\PYZus{}mse}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{shape}\PY{p}{[}\PY{l+m+mi}{0}\PY{p}{]}
\PY{n}{ax}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{plot}\PY{p}{(}\PY{n}{np}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{arange}\PY{p}{(}\PY{n}{n\PYZus{}steps}\PY{p}{)}\PY{p}{,}
        \PY{n}{insample\PYZus{}mse}\PY{p}{,}
        \PY{l+s+s1}{\PYZsq{}}\PY{l+s+s1}{k}\PY{l+s+s1}{\PYZsq{}}\PY{p}{,} \PY{c+c1}{\PYZsh{} color black}
        \PY{n}{label}\PY{o}{=}\PY{l+s+s1}{\PYZsq{}}\PY{l+s+s1}{In\PYZhy{}sample}\PY{l+s+s1}{\PYZsq{}}\PY{p}{)}
\PY{n}{ax}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{set\PYZus{}ylabel}\PY{p}{(}\PY{l+s+s1}{\PYZsq{}}\PY{l+s+s1}{MSE}\PY{l+s+s1}{\PYZsq{}}\PY{p}{,}
              \PY{n}{fontsize}\PY{o}{=}\PY{l+m+mi}{20}\PY{p}{)}
\PY{n}{ax}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{set\PYZus{}xlabel}\PY{p}{(}\PY{l+s+s1}{\PYZsq{}}\PY{l+s+s1}{\PYZsh{} steps of forward stepwise}\PY{l+s+s1}{\PYZsq{}}\PY{p}{,}
              \PY{n}{fontsize}\PY{o}{=}\PY{l+m+mi}{20}\PY{p}{)}
\PY{n}{ax}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{set\PYZus{}xticks}\PY{p}{(}\PY{n}{np}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{arange}\PY{p}{(}\PY{n}{n\PYZus{}steps}\PY{p}{)}\PY{p}{[}\PY{p}{:}\PY{p}{:}\PY{l+m+mi}{2}\PY{p}{]}\PY{p}{)}
\PY{n}{ax}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{legend}\PY{p}{(}\PY{p}{)}
\PY{n}{ax}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{set\PYZus{}ylim}\PY{p}{(}\PY{p}{[}\PY{l+m+mi}{50000}\PY{p}{,}\PY{l+m+mi}{250000}\PY{p}{]}\PY{p}{)}\PY{p}{;}
\end{Verbatim}
\end{tcolorbox}

    \begin{center}
    \adjustimage{max size={0.9\linewidth}{0.9\paperheight}}{artifacts/latex/Ch06-varselect-lab_files/artifacts/latex/Ch06-varselect-lab_28_0.png}
    \end{center}
    { \hspace*{\fill} \\}
    
    Notice the expression \texttt{None} in \texttt{Y{[}:,None{]}} above.
This adds an axis (dimension) to the one-dimensional array \texttt{Y},
which allows it to be recycled when subtracted from the two-dimensional
\texttt{Yhat\_in}.

    We are now ready to use cross-validation to estimate test error along
the model path. We must use \emph{only the training observations} to
perform all aspects of model-fitting --- including variable selection.
Therefore, the determination of which model of a given size is best must
be made using \emph{only the training
  observations} in each training fold. This point is subtle but
important. If the full data set is used to select the best subset at
each step, then the validation set errors and cross-validation errors
that we obtain will not be accurate estimates of the test error.

We now compute the cross-validated predicted values using 5-fold
cross-validation.

    \begin{tcolorbox}[breakable, size=fbox, boxrule=1pt, pad at break*=1mm,colback=cellbackground, colframe=cellborder]
\prompt{In}{incolor}{14}{\boxspacing}
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PY{n}{K} \PY{o}{=} \PY{l+m+mi}{5}
\PY{n}{kfold} \PY{o}{=} \PY{n}{skm}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{KFold}\PY{p}{(}\PY{n}{K}\PY{p}{,}
                  \PY{n}{random\PYZus{}state}\PY{o}{=}\PY{l+m+mi}{0}\PY{p}{,}
                  \PY{n}{shuffle}\PY{o}{=}\PY{k+kc}{True}\PY{p}{)}
\PY{n}{Yhat\PYZus{}cv} \PY{o}{=} \PY{n}{skm}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{cross\PYZus{}val\PYZus{}predict}\PY{p}{(}\PY{n}{full\PYZus{}path}\PY{p}{,}
                                \PY{n}{Hitters}\PY{p}{,}
                                \PY{n}{Y}\PY{p}{,}
                                \PY{n}{cv}\PY{o}{=}\PY{n}{kfold}\PY{p}{)}
\PY{n}{Yhat\PYZus{}cv}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{shape}
\end{Verbatim}
\end{tcolorbox}

            \begin{tcolorbox}[breakable, size=fbox, boxrule=.5pt, pad at break*=1mm, opacityfill=0]
\prompt{Out}{outcolor}{14}{\boxspacing}

    \texttt{skm.cross\_val\_predict()} The prediction matrix
\texttt{Yhat\_cv} is the same shape as \texttt{Yhat\_in}; the difference
is that the predictions in each row, corresponding to a particular
sample index, were made from models fit on a training fold that did not
include that row.

At each model along the path, we compute the MSE in each of the
cross-validation folds. These we will average to get the mean MSE, and
can also use the individual values to compute a crude estimate of the
standard error of the mean. \{The estimate is crude because the five
error estimates are based on overlapping training sets, and hence are
not independent.\} Hence we must know the test indices for each
cross-validation split. This can be found by using the \texttt{split()}
method of \texttt{kfold}. Because we fixed the random state above,
whenever we split any array with the same number of rows as \(Y\) we
recover the same training and test indices, though we simply ignore the
training indices below.

    \begin{tcolorbox}[breakable, size=fbox, boxrule=1pt, pad at break*=1mm,colback=cellbackground, colframe=cellborder]
\prompt{In}{incolor}{15}{\boxspacing}
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PY{n}{cv\PYZus{}mse} \PY{o}{=} \PY{p}{[}\PY{p}{]}
\PY{k}{for} \PY{n}{train\PYZus{}idx}\PY{p}{,} \PY{n}{test\PYZus{}idx} \PY{o+ow}{in} \PY{n}{kfold}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{split}\PY{p}{(}\PY{n}{Y}\PY{p}{)}\PY{p}{:}
    \PY{n}{errors} \PY{o}{=} \PY{p}{(}\PY{n}{Yhat\PYZus{}cv}\PY{p}{[}\PY{n}{test\PYZus{}idx}\PY{p}{]} \PY{o}{\PYZhy{}} \PY{n}{Y}\PY{p}{[}\PY{n}{test\PYZus{}idx}\PY{p}{,}\PY{k+kc}{None}\PY{p}{]}\PY{p}{)}\PY{o}{*}\PY{o}{*}\PY{l+m+mi}{2}
    \PY{n}{cv\PYZus{}mse}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{append}\PY{p}{(}\PY{n}{errors}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{mean}\PY{p}{(}\PY{l+m+mi}{0}\PY{p}{)}\PY{p}{)} \PY{c+c1}{\PYZsh{} column means}
\PY{n}{cv\PYZus{}mse} \PY{o}{=} \PY{n}{np}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{array}\PY{p}{(}\PY{n}{cv\PYZus{}mse}\PY{p}{)}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{T}
\PY{n}{cv\PYZus{}mse}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{shape}
\end{Verbatim}
\end{tcolorbox}

            \begin{tcolorbox}[breakable, size=fbox, boxrule=.5pt, pad at break*=1mm, opacityfill=0]
\prompt{Out}{outcolor}{15}{\boxspacing}
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
(20, 5)
\end{Verbatim}
\end{tcolorbox}
        
    We now add the cross-validation error estimates to our MSE plot. We
include the mean error across the five folds, and the estimate of the
standard error of the mean.

    \begin{tcolorbox}[breakable, size=fbox, boxrule=1pt, pad at break*=1mm,colback=cellbackground, colframe=cellborder]
\prompt{In}{incolor}{16}{\boxspacing}

            \PY{n}{cv\PYZus{}mse}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{mean}\PY{p}{(}\PY{l+m+mi}{1}\PY{p}{)}\PY{p}{,}

\PY{n}{ax}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{set\PYZus{}ylim}\PY{p}{(}\PY{p}{[}\PY{l+m+mi}{50000}\PY{p}{,}\PY{l+m+mi}{250000}\PY{p}{]}\PY{p}{)}

    \hypertarget{best-subset-selection}{%
\subsubsection{Best Subset Selection}\label{best-subset-selection}}

Forward stepwise is a \emph{greedy} selection procedure; at each step it
augments the current set by including one additional variable. We now
apply best subset selection to the \texttt{Hitters} data, which for
every subset size, searches for the best set of predictors.

We will use a package called \texttt{l0bnb} to perform best subset
selection. Instead of constraining the subset to be a given size, this
package produces a path of solutions using the subset size as a penalty
rather than a constraint. Although the distinction is subtle, the
difference comes when we cross-validate.

    \begin{tcolorbox}[breakable, size=fbox, boxrule=1pt, pad at break*=1mm,colback=cellbackground, colframe=cellborder]
\prompt{In}{incolor}{19}{\boxspacing}
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PY{n}{D} \PY{o}{=} \PY{n}{design}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{fit\PYZus{}transform}\PY{p}{(}\PY{n}{Hitters}\PY{p}{)}
\PY{n}{D} \PY{o}{=} \PY{n}{D}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{drop}\PY{p}{(}\PY{l+s+s1}{\PYZsq{}}\PY{l+s+s1}{intercept}\PY{l+s+s1}{\PYZsq{}}\PY{p}{,} \PY{n}{axis}\PY{o}{=}\PY{l+m+mi}{1}\PY{p}{)}
\PY{n}{X} \PY{o}{=} \PY{n}{np}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{asarray}\PY{p}{(}\PY{n}{D}\PY{p}{)}
\end{Verbatim}
\end{tcolorbox}

    Here we excluded the first column corresponding to the intercept, as
\texttt{l0bnb} will fit the intercept separately. We can find a path
using the \texttt{fit\_path()} function.

                \PY{n}{Y}\PY{p}{,}
                \PY{n}{max\PYZus{}nonzeros}\PY{o}{=}\PY{n}{X}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{shape}\PY{p}{[}\PY{l+m+mi}{1}\PY{p}{]}\PY{p}{)}
\end{Verbatim}
\end{tcolorbox}

    The function \texttt{fit\_path()} returns a list whose values include
the fitted coefficients as \texttt{B}, an intercept as \texttt{B0}, as
well as a few other attributes related to the particular path algorithm
used. Such details are beyond the scope of this book.

        0.        , 0.        , 0.        , 0.        , 0.        ,
        0.        , 0.67775265, 0.        , 0.        , 0.        ,
        0.        , 0.        , 0.        , 0.        ]),

    In the example above, we see that at the fourth step in the path, we
have two nonzero coefficients in
\texttt{\textquotesingle{}B\textquotesingle{}}, corresponding to the
value \(0.0114\) for the penalty parameter \texttt{lambda\_0}. We could
make predictions using this sequence of fits on a validation set as a
function of \texttt{lambda\_0}, or with more work using
cross-validation.

\hypertarget{ridge-regression-and-the-lasso}{%
\subsection{Ridge Regression and the
Lasso}\label{ridge-regression-and-the-lasso}}

We will use the \texttt{sklearn.linear\_model} package (for which we use
\texttt{skl} as shorthand below) to fit ridge and lasso regularized
linear models on the \texttt{Hitters} data. We start with the model
matrix \texttt{X} (without an intercept) that we computed in the
previous section on best subset regression.

\hypertarget{ridge-regression}{%
\subsubsection{Ridge Regression}\label{ridge-regression}}

We will use the function \texttt{skl.ElasticNet()} to fit both ridge and
the lasso. To fit a \emph{path} of ridge regressions models, we use
\texttt{skl.ElasticNet.path()}, which can fit both ridge and lasso, as
well as a hybrid mixture; ridge regression corresponds to
\texttt{l1\_ratio=0}. It is good practice to standardize the columns of
\texttt{X} in these applications, if the variables are measured in
different units. Since \texttt{skl.ElasticNet()} does no normalization,
we have to take care of that ourselves. Since we standardize first, in
order to find coefficient estimates on the original scale, we must
\emph{unstandardize} the coefficient estimates. The parameter
\(\lambda\) in (6.5) and (6.7) is called \texttt{alphas} in
\texttt{sklearn}. In order to be consistent with the rest of this
chapter, we use \texttt{lambdas} rather than \texttt{alphas} in what
follows. \{At the time of publication, ridge fits like the one in code
chunk {[}22{]} issue unwarranted convergence warning messages; we expect
these to disappear as this package matures.\}

            \begin{tcolorbox}[breakable, size=fbox, boxrule=.5pt, pad at break*=1mm, opacityfill=0]
\prompt{Out}{outcolor}{22}{\boxspacing}
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
(19, 100)

\end{tcolorbox}
        
    Here we extract the array of coefficients corresponding to the solutions
along the regularization path. By default the
\texttt{skl.ElasticNet.path} method fits a path along an automatically
selected range of \(\lambda\) values, except for the case when
\texttt{l1\_ratio=0}, which results in ridge regression (as is the case
here). \{The reason is rather technical; for all models except ridge, we
can find the smallest value of \(\lambda\) for which all coefficients
are zero. For ridge this value is \(\infty\).\} So here we have chosen
to implement the function over a grid of values ranging from
\(\lambda=10^{8}\) to \(\lambda=10^{-2}\) scaled by the standard
deviation of \(y\), essentially covering the full range of scenarios
from the null model containing only the intercept, to the least squares
fit.

Associated with each value of \(\lambda\) is a vector of ridge
regression coefficients, that can be accessed by a column of
\texttt{soln\_array}. In this case, \texttt{soln\_array} is a
\(19 \times 100\) matrix, with 19 rows (one for each predictor) and 100
columns (one for each value of \(\lambda\)).

We transpose this matrix and turn it into a data frame to facilitate
viewing and plotting.

    \begin{tcolorbox}[breakable, size=fbox, boxrule=1pt, pad at break*=1mm,colback=cellbackground, colframe=cellborder]
\prompt{In}{incolor}{23}{\boxspacing}
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PY{n}{soln\PYZus{}path} \PY{o}{=} \PY{n}{pd}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{DataFrame}\PY{p}{(}\PY{n}{soln\PYZus{}array}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{T}\PY{p}{,}
                         \PY{n}{columns}\PY{o}{=}\PY{n}{D}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{columns}\PY{p}{,}
                         \PY{n}{index}\PY{o}{=}\PY{o}{\PYZhy{}}\PY{n}{np}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{log}\PY{p}{(}\PY{n}{lambdas}\PY{p}{)}\PY{p}{)}
\PY{n}{soln\PYZus{}path}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{index}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{name} \PY{o}{=} \PY{l+s+s1}{\PYZsq{}}\PY{l+s+s1}{negative log(lambda)}\PY{l+s+s1}{\PYZsq{}}
\PY{n}{soln\PYZus{}path}
\end{Verbatim}
\end{tcolorbox}

\(\lambda\). To control the location of the legend we first set
\texttt{legend} to \texttt{False} in the plot method, adding it
afterward with the \texttt{legend()} method of \texttt{ax}.

    Notice that the operation \texttt{pipe.fit(X,\ Y)} above has changed the
\texttt{ridge} object, and in particular has added attributes such as
\texttt{coef\_} that were not there before. \#\#\# Estimating Test Error
of Ridge Regression Choosing an \emph{a priori} value of \(\lambda\) for
ridge regression is difficult if not impossible. We will want to use the
validation method or cross-validation to select the tuning parameter.
The reader may not be surprised that the \texttt{Pipeline()} approach
can be used in \texttt{skm.cross\_validate()} with either a validation
method (i.e.~\texttt{validation}) or \(k\)-fold cross-validation.

We fix the random state of the splitter so that the results obtained
will be reproducible.

    \begin{tcolorbox}[breakable, size=fbox, boxrule=1pt, pad at break*=1mm,colback=cellbackground, colframe=cellborder]

                              \PY{n}{test\PYZus{}size}\PY{o}{=}\PY{l+m+mf}{0.5}\PY{p}{,}
                              \PY{n}{random\PYZus{}state}\PY{o}{=}\PY{l+m+mi}{0}\PY{p}{)}
\PY{n}{ridge}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{alpha} \PY{o}{=} \PY{l+m+mf}{0.01}
\PY{n}{results} \PY{o}{=} \PY{n}{skm}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{cross\PYZus{}validate}\PY{p}{(}\PY{n}{ridge}\PY{p}{,}

                             \PY{n}{Y}\PY{p}{,}
                             \PY{n}{scoring}\PY{o}{=}\PY{l+s+s1}{\PYZsq{}}\PY{l+s+s1}{neg\PYZus{}mean\PYZus{}squared\PYZus{}error}\PY{l+s+s1}{\PYZsq{}}\PY{p}{,}
                             \PY{n}{cv}\PY{o}{=}\PY{n}{validation}\PY{p}{)}
\PY{o}{\PYZhy{}}\PY{n}{results}\PY{p}{[}\PY{l+s+s1}{\PYZsq{}}\PY{l+s+s1}{test\PYZus{}score}\PY{l+s+s1}{\PYZsq{}}\PY{p}{]}

    \hypertarget{fast-cross-validation-for-solution-paths}{%
\subsubsection{Fast Cross-Validation for Solution
Paths}\label{fast-cross-validation-for-solution-paths}}

The ridge, lasso, and elastic net can be efficiently fit along a
sequence of \(\lambda\) values, creating what is known as a
\emph{solution path} or \emph{regularization path}. Hence there is
specialized code to fit such paths, and to choose a suitable value of
\(\lambda\) using cross-validation. Even with identical splits the
results will not agree \emph{exactly} with our \texttt{grid} above
because the standardization of each feature in \texttt{grid} is carried
out on each fold, while in \texttt{pipeCV} below it is carried out only
once. Nevertheless, the results are similar as the normalization is
relatively stable across folds.

                           \PY{n}{l1\PYZus{}ratio}\PY{o}{=}\PY{l+m+mi}{0}\PY{p}{,}
                           \PY{n}{cv}\PY{o}{=}\PY{n}{kfold}\PY{p}{)}
\PY{n}{pipeCV} \PY{o}{=} \PY{n}{Pipeline}\PY{p}{(}\PY{n}{steps}\PY{o}{=}\PY{p}{[}\PY{p}{(}\PY{l+s+s1}{\PYZsq{}}\PY{l+s+s1}{scaler}\PY{l+s+s1}{\PYZsq{}}\PY{p}{,} \PY{n}{scaler}\PY{p}{)}\PY{p}{,}
                         \PY{p}{(}\PY{l+s+s1}{\PYZsq{}}\PY{l+s+s1}{ridge}\PY{l+s+s1}{\PYZsq{}}\PY{p}{,} \PY{n}{ridgeCV}\PY{p}{)}\PY{p}{]}\PY{p}{)}

    \hypertarget{evaluating-test-error-of-cross-validated-ridge}{%
\subsubsection{Evaluating Test Error of Cross-Validated
Ridge}\label{evaluating-test-error-of-cross-validated-ridge}}

Choosing \(\lambda\) using cross-validation provides a single regression
estimator, similar to fitting a linear regression model as we saw in
Chapter 3. It is therefore reasonable to estimate what its test error
is. We run into a problem here in that cross-validation will have
\emph{touched} all of its data in choosing \(\lambda\), hence we have no
further data to estimate test error. A compromise is to do an initial
split of the data into two disjoint sets: a training set and a test set.
We then fit a cross-validation tuned ridge regression on the training
set, and evaluate its performance on the test set. We might call this
cross-validation nested within the validation set approach. A priori
there is no reason to use half of the data for each of the two sets in
validation. Below, we use 75\% for training and 25\% for test, with the
estimator being ridge regression tuned using 5-fold cross-validation.
This can be achieved in code as follows:

    \begin{tcolorbox}[breakable, size=fbox, boxrule=1pt, pad at break*=1mm,colback=cellbackground, colframe=cellborder]
\prompt{In}{incolor}{41}{\boxspacing}
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PY{n}{outer\PYZus{}valid} \PY{o}{=} \PY{n}{skm}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{ShuffleSplit}\PY{p}{(}\PY{n}{n\PYZus{}splits}\PY{o}{=}\PY{l+m+mi}{1}\PY{p}{,} 
                               \PY{n}{test\PYZus{}size}\PY{o}{=}\PY{l+m+mf}{0.25}\PY{p}{,}
                               \PY{n}{random\PYZus{}state}\PY{o}{=}\PY{l+m+mi}{1}\PY{p}{)}
\PY{n}{inner\PYZus{}cv} \PY{o}{=} \PY{n}{skm}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{KFold}\PY{p}{(}\PY{n}{n\PYZus{}splits}\PY{o}{=}\PY{l+m+mi}{5}\PY{p}{,}
                     \PY{n}{shuffle}\PY{o}{=}\PY{k+kc}{True}\PY{p}{,}
                     \PY{n}{random\PYZus{}state}\PY{o}{=}\PY{l+m+mi}{2}\PY{p}{)}
\PY{n}{ridgeCV} \PY{o}{=} \PY{n}{skl}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{ElasticNetCV}\PY{p}{(}\PY{n}{alphas}\PY{o}{=}\PY{n}{lambdas}\PY{p}{,}
                           \PY{n}{l1\PYZus{}ratio}\PY{o}{=}\PY{l+m+mi}{0}\PY{p}{,}
                           \PY{n}{cv}\PY{o}{=}\PY{n}{inner\PYZus{}cv}\PY{p}{)}
\PY{n}{pipeCV} \PY{o}{=} \PY{n}{Pipeline}\PY{p}{(}\PY{n}{steps}\PY{o}{=}\PY{p}{[}\PY{p}{(}\PY{l+s+s1}{\PYZsq{}}\PY{l+s+s1}{scaler}\PY{l+s+s1}{\PYZsq{}}\PY{p}{,} \PY{n}{scaler}\PY{p}{)}\PY{p}{,}
                         \PY{p}{(}\PY{l+s+s1}{\PYZsq{}}\PY{l+s+s1}{ridge}\PY{l+s+s1}{\PYZsq{}}\PY{p}{,} \PY{n}{ridgeCV}\PY{p}{)}\PY{p}{]}\PY{p}{)}\PY{p}{;}
\end{Verbatim}
\end{tcolorbox}

    \hypertarget{the-lasso}{%
\subsubsection{The Lasso}\label{the-lasso}}

We saw that ridge regression with a wise choice of \(\lambda\) can
outperform least squares as well as the null model on the
\texttt{Hitters} data set. We now ask whether the lasso can yield either
a more accurate or a more interpretable model than ridge regression. In
order to fit a lasso model, we once again use the
\texttt{ElasticNetCV()} function; however, this time we use the argument
\texttt{l1\_ratio=1}. Other than that change, we proceed just as we did
in fitting a ridge model.

    \begin{tcolorbox}[breakable, size=fbox, boxrule=1pt, pad at break*=1mm,colback=cellbackground, colframe=cellborder]
\prompt{In}{incolor}{43}{\boxspacing}
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PY{n}{lassoCV} \PY{o}{=} \PY{n}{skl}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{ElasticNetCV}\PY{p}{(}\PY{n}{n\PYZus{}alphas}\PY{o}{=}\PY{l+m+mi}{100}\PY{p}{,} 
                           \PY{n}{l1\PYZus{}ratio}\PY{o}{=}\PY{l+m+mi}{1}\PY{p}{,}
                           \PY{n}{cv}\PY{o}{=}\PY{n}{kfold}\PY{p}{)}
\PY{n}{pipeCV} \PY{o}{=} \PY{n}{Pipeline}\PY{p}{(}\PY{n}{steps}\PY{o}{=}\PY{p}{[}\PY{p}{(}\PY{l+s+s1}{\PYZsq{}}\PY{l+s+s1}{scaler}\PY{l+s+s1}{\PYZsq{}}\PY{p}{,} \PY{n}{scaler}\PY{p}{)}\PY{p}{,}
                         \PY{p}{(}\PY{l+s+s1}{\PYZsq{}}\PY{l+s+s1}{lasso}\PY{l+s+s1}{\PYZsq{}}\PY{p}{,} \PY{n}{lassoCV}\PY{p}{)}\PY{p}{]}\PY{p}{)}
\PY{n}{pipeCV}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{fit}\PY{p}{(}\PY{n}{X}\PY{p}{,} \PY{n}{Y}\PY{p}{)}
\PY{n}{tuned\PYZus{}lasso} \PY{o}{=} \PY{n}{pipeCV}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{named\PYZus{}steps}\PY{p}{[}\PY{l+s+s1}{\PYZsq{}}\PY{l+s+s1}{lasso}\PY{l+s+s1}{\PYZsq{}}\PY{p}{]}
\PY{n}{tuned\PYZus{}lasso}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{alpha\PYZus{}}

                                    \PY{n}{n\PYZus{}alphas}\PY{o}{=}\PY{l+m+mi}{100}\PY{p}{)}\PY{p}{[}\PY{p}{:}\PY{l+m+mi}{2}\PY{p}{]}

                         \PY{n}{columns}\PY{o}{=}\PY{n}{D}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{columns}\PY{p}{,}
                         \PY{n}{index}\PY{o}{=}\PY{o}{\PYZhy{}}\PY{n}{np}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{log}\PY{p}{(}\PY{n}{lambdas}\PY{p}{)}\PY{p}{)}
\end{Verbatim}
\end{tcolorbox}

    We can see from the coefficient plot of the standardized coefficients
that depending on the choice of tuning parameter, some of the
coefficients will be exactly equal to zero.

    \hypertarget{pcr-and-pls-regression}{%
\subsection{PCR and PLS Regression}\label{pcr-and-pls-regression}}

\hypertarget{principal-components-regression}{%
\subsubsection{Principal Components
Regression}\label{principal-components-regression}}

    Principal components regression (PCR) can be performed using
\texttt{PCA()} from the \texttt{sklearn.decomposition} module. We now
apply PCR to the \texttt{Hitters} data, in order to predict
\texttt{Salary}. Again, ensure that the missing values have been removed
from the data, as described in Section 6.5.1.

We use \texttt{LinearRegression()} to fit the regression model here.
Note that it fits an intercept by default, unlike the \texttt{OLS()}
function seen earlier in Section 6.5.1.

    \begin{tcolorbox}[breakable, size=fbox, boxrule=1pt, pad at break*=1mm,colback=cellbackground, colframe=cellborder]
\prompt{In}{incolor}{49}{\boxspacing}
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PY{n}{pca} \PY{o}{=} \PY{n}{PCA}\PY{p}{(}\PY{n}{n\PYZus{}components}\PY{o}{=}\PY{l+m+mi}{2}\PY{p}{)}
\PY{n}{linreg} \PY{o}{=} \PY{n}{skl}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{LinearRegression}\PY{p}{(}\PY{p}{)}
\PY{n}{pipe} \PY{o}{=} \PY{n}{Pipeline}\PY{p}{(}\PY{p}{[}\PY{p}{(}\PY{l+s+s1}{\PYZsq{}}\PY{l+s+s1}{pca}\PY{l+s+s1}{\PYZsq{}}\PY{p}{,} \PY{n}{pca}\PY{p}{)}\PY{p}{,}
                 \PY{p}{(}\PY{l+s+s1}{\PYZsq{}}\PY{l+s+s1}{linreg}\PY{l+s+s1}{\PYZsq{}}\PY{p}{,} \PY{n}{linreg}\PY{p}{)}\PY{p}{]}\PY{p}{)}
\PY{n}{pipe}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{fit}\PY{p}{(}\PY{n}{X}\PY{p}{,} \PY{n}{Y}\PY{p}{)}
\PY{n}{pipe}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{named\PYZus{}steps}\PY{p}{[}\PY{l+s+s1}{\PYZsq{}}\PY{l+s+s1}{linreg}\PY{l+s+s1}{\PYZsq{}}\PY{p}{]}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{coef\PYZus{}}
\end{Verbatim}
\end{tcolorbox}

            \begin{tcolorbox}[breakable, size=fbox, boxrule=.5pt, pad at break*=1mm, opacityfill=0]
\prompt{Out}{outcolor}{49}{\boxspacing}
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
array([0.09846131, 0.4758765 ])
\end{Verbatim}
\end{tcolorbox}
        
    When performing PCA, the results vary depending on whether the data has
been \emph{standardized} or not. As in the earlier examples, this can be
accomplished by including an additional step in the pipeline.

    \begin{tcolorbox}[breakable, size=fbox, boxrule=1pt, pad at break*=1mm,colback=cellbackground, colframe=cellborder]
\prompt{In}{incolor}{50}{\boxspacing}
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PY{n}{pipe} \PY{o}{=} \PY{n}{Pipeline}\PY{p}{(}\PY{p}{[}\PY{p}{(}\PY{l+s+s1}{\PYZsq{}}\PY{l+s+s1}{scaler}\PY{l+s+s1}{\PYZsq{}}\PY{p}{,} \PY{n}{scaler}\PY{p}{)}\PY{p}{,} 
                 \PY{p}{(}\PY{l+s+s1}{\PYZsq{}}\PY{l+s+s1}{pca}\PY{l+s+s1}{\PYZsq{}}\PY{p}{,} \PY{n}{pca}\PY{p}{)}\PY{p}{,}
                 \PY{p}{(}\PY{l+s+s1}{\PYZsq{}}\PY{l+s+s1}{linreg}\PY{l+s+s1}{\PYZsq{}}\PY{p}{,} \PY{n}{linreg}\PY{p}{)}\PY{p}{]}\PY{p}{)}
\PY{n}{pipe}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{fit}\PY{p}{(}\PY{n}{X}\PY{p}{,} \PY{n}{Y}\PY{p}{)}
\PY{n}{pipe}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{named\PYZus{}steps}\PY{p}{[}\PY{l+s+s1}{\PYZsq{}}\PY{l+s+s1}{linreg}\PY{l+s+s1}{\PYZsq{}}\PY{p}{]}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{coef\PYZus{}}
\end{Verbatim}
\end{tcolorbox}

            \begin{tcolorbox}[breakable, size=fbox, boxrule=.5pt, pad at break*=1mm, opacityfill=0]
\prompt{Out}{outcolor}{50}{\boxspacing}
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
array([106.36859204,  21.60350456])
\end{Verbatim}
\end{tcolorbox}
        
    We can of course use CV to choose the number of components, by using
\texttt{skm.GridSearchCV}, in this case fixing the parameters to vary
the \texttt{n\_components}.

    \begin{tcolorbox}[breakable, size=fbox, boxrule=1pt, pad at break*=1mm,colback=cellbackground, colframe=cellborder]
\prompt{In}{incolor}{51}{\boxspacing}
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PY{n}{param\PYZus{}grid} \PY{o}{=} \PY{p}{\PYZob{}}\PY{l+s+s1}{\PYZsq{}}\PY{l+s+s1}{pca\PYZus{}\PYZus{}n\PYZus{}components}\PY{l+s+s1}{\PYZsq{}}\PY{p}{:} \PY{n+nb}{range}\PY{p}{(}\PY{l+m+mi}{1}\PY{p}{,} \PY{l+m+mi}{20}\PY{p}{)}\PY{p}{\PYZcb{}}
\PY{n}{grid} \PY{o}{=} \PY{n}{skm}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{GridSearchCV}\PY{p}{(}\PY{n}{pipe}\PY{p}{,}
                        \PY{n}{param\PYZus{}grid}\PY{p}{,}
                        \PY{n}{cv}\PY{o}{=}\PY{n}{kfold}\PY{p}{,}
                        \PY{n}{scoring}\PY{o}{=}\PY{l+s+s1}{\PYZsq{}}\PY{l+s+s1}{neg\PYZus{}mean\PYZus{}squared\PYZus{}error}\PY{l+s+s1}{\PYZsq{}}\PY{p}{)}
\PY{n}{grid}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{fit}\PY{p}{(}\PY{n}{X}\PY{p}{,} \PY{n}{Y}\PY{p}{)}
\end{Verbatim}
\end{tcolorbox}

            \begin{tcolorbox}[breakable, size=fbox, boxrule=.5pt, pad at break*=1mm, opacityfill=0]
\prompt{Out}{outcolor}{51}{\boxspacing}
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
GridSearchCV(cv=KFold(n\_splits=5, random\_state=0, shuffle=True),
             estimator=Pipeline(steps=[('scaler', StandardScaler()),
                                       ('pca', PCA(n\_components=2)),
                                       ('linreg', LinearRegression())]),
             param\_grid=\{'pca\_\_n\_components': range(1, 20)\},
             scoring='neg\_mean\_squared\_error')
\end{Verbatim}
\end{tcolorbox}
        
    Let's plot the results as we have for other methods.

    \begin{tcolorbox}[breakable, size=fbox, boxrule=1pt, pad at break*=1mm,colback=cellbackground, colframe=cellborder]
\prompt{In}{incolor}{52}{\boxspacing}
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PY{n}{pcr\PYZus{}fig}\PY{p}{,} \PY{n}{ax} \PY{o}{=} \PY{n}{subplots}\PY{p}{(}\PY{n}{figsize}\PY{o}{=}\PY{p}{(}\PY{l+m+mi}{8}\PY{p}{,}\PY{l+m+mi}{8}\PY{p}{)}\PY{p}{)}
\PY{n}{n\PYZus{}comp} \PY{o}{=} \PY{n}{param\PYZus{}grid}\PY{p}{[}\PY{l+s+s1}{\PYZsq{}}\PY{l+s+s1}{pca\PYZus{}\PYZus{}n\PYZus{}components}\PY{l+s+s1}{\PYZsq{}}\PY{p}{]}
\PY{n}{ax}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{errorbar}\PY{p}{(}\PY{n}{n\PYZus{}comp}\PY{p}{,}
            \PY{o}{\PYZhy{}}\PY{n}{grid}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{cv\PYZus{}results\PYZus{}}\PY{p}{[}\PY{l+s+s1}{\PYZsq{}}\PY{l+s+s1}{mean\PYZus{}test\PYZus{}score}\PY{l+s+s1}{\PYZsq{}}\PY{p}{]}\PY{p}{,}
            \PY{n}{grid}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{cv\PYZus{}results\PYZus{}}\PY{p}{[}\PY{l+s+s1}{\PYZsq{}}\PY{l+s+s1}{std\PYZus{}test\PYZus{}score}\PY{l+s+s1}{\PYZsq{}}\PY{p}{]} \PY{o}{/} \PY{n}{np}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{sqrt}\PY{p}{(}\PY{n}{K}\PY{p}{)}\PY{p}{)}
\PY{n}{ax}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{set\PYZus{}ylabel}\PY{p}{(}\PY{l+s+s1}{\PYZsq{}}\PY{l+s+s1}{Cross\PYZhy{}validated MSE}\PY{l+s+s1}{\PYZsq{}}\PY{p}{,} \PY{n}{fontsize}\PY{o}{=}\PY{l+m+mi}{20}\PY{p}{)}
\PY{n}{ax}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{set\PYZus{}xlabel}\PY{p}{(}\PY{l+s+s1}{\PYZsq{}}\PY{l+s+s1}{\PYZsh{} principal components}\PY{l+s+s1}{\PYZsq{}}\PY{p}{,} \PY{n}{fontsize}\PY{o}{=}\PY{l+m+mi}{20}\PY{p}{)}
\PY{n}{ax}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{set\PYZus{}xticks}\PY{p}{(}\PY{n}{n\PYZus{}comp}\PY{p}{[}\PY{p}{:}\PY{p}{:}\PY{l+m+mi}{2}\PY{p}{]}\PY{p}{)}
\PY{n}{ax}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{set\PYZus{}ylim}\PY{p}{(}\PY{p}{[}\PY{l+m+mi}{50000}\PY{p}{,}\PY{l+m+mi}{250000}\PY{p}{]}\PY{p}{)}\PY{p}{;}
\end{Verbatim}
\end{tcolorbox}

    \begin{center}
    \adjustimage{max size={0.9\linewidth}{0.9\paperheight}}{artifacts/latex/Ch06-varselect-lab_files/artifacts/latex/Ch06-varselect-lab_109_0.png}
    \end{center}
    { \hspace*{\fill} \\}
    
    We see that the smallest cross-validation error occurs when 17
components are used. However, from the plot we also see that the
cross-validation error is roughly the same when only one component is
included in the model. This suggests that a model that uses just a small
number of components might suffice.

The CV score is provided for each possible number of components from 1
to 19 inclusive. The \texttt{PCA()} method complains if we try to fit an
intercept only with \texttt{n\_components=0} so we also compute the MSE
for just the null model with these splits.

    \begin{tcolorbox}[breakable, size=fbox, boxrule=1pt, pad at break*=1mm,colback=cellbackground, colframe=cellborder]
\prompt{In}{incolor}{53}{\boxspacing}
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PY{n}{Xn} \PY{o}{=} \PY{n}{np}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{zeros}\PY{p}{(}\PY{p}{(}\PY{n}{X}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{shape}\PY{p}{[}\PY{l+m+mi}{0}\PY{p}{]}\PY{p}{,} \PY{l+m+mi}{1}\PY{p}{)}\PY{p}{)}
\PY{n}{cv\PYZus{}null} \PY{o}{=} \PY{n}{skm}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{cross\PYZus{}validate}\PY{p}{(}\PY{n}{linreg}\PY{p}{,}
                             \PY{n}{Xn}\PY{p}{,}
                             \PY{n}{Y}\PY{p}{,}
                             \PY{n}{cv}\PY{o}{=}\PY{n}{kfold}\PY{p}{,}
                             \PY{n}{scoring}\PY{o}{=}\PY{l+s+s1}{\PYZsq{}}\PY{l+s+s1}{neg\PYZus{}mean\PYZus{}squared\PYZus{}error}\PY{l+s+s1}{\PYZsq{}}\PY{p}{)}
\PY{o}{\PYZhy{}}\PY{n}{cv\PYZus{}null}\PY{p}{[}\PY{l+s+s1}{\PYZsq{}}\PY{l+s+s1}{test\PYZus{}score}\PY{l+s+s1}{\PYZsq{}}\PY{p}{]}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{mean}\PY{p}{(}\PY{p}{)}
\end{Verbatim}
\end{tcolorbox}

            \begin{tcolorbox}[breakable, size=fbox, boxrule=.5pt, pad at break*=1mm, opacityfill=0]
\prompt{Out}{outcolor}{53}{\boxspacing}
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
204139.30692994667
\end{Verbatim}
\end{tcolorbox}
        
    The \texttt{explained\_variance\_ratio\_} attribute of our \texttt{PCA}
object provides the \emph{percentage of variance explained} in the
predictors and in the response using different numbers of components.
This concept is discussed in greater detail in Section 12.2.

    \begin{tcolorbox}[breakable, size=fbox, boxrule=1pt, pad at break*=1mm,colback=cellbackground, colframe=cellborder]
\prompt{In}{incolor}{54}{\boxspacing}
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PY{n}{pipe}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{named\PYZus{}steps}\PY{p}{[}\PY{l+s+s1}{\PYZsq{}}\PY{l+s+s1}{pca}\PY{l+s+s1}{\PYZsq{}}\PY{p}{]}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{explained\PYZus{}variance\PYZus{}ratio\PYZus{}}
\end{Verbatim}
\end{tcolorbox}

            \begin{tcolorbox}[breakable, size=fbox, boxrule=.5pt, pad at break*=1mm, opacityfill=0]
\prompt{Out}{outcolor}{54}{\boxspacing}
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
array([0.3831424 , 0.21841076])
\end{Verbatim}
\end{tcolorbox}
        
    Briefly, we can think of this as the amount of information about the
predictors that is captured using \(M\) principal components. For
example, setting \(M=1\) only captures 38.31\% of the variance, while
\(M=2\) captures an additional 21.84\%, for a total of 60.15\% of the
variance. By \(M=6\) it increases to 88.63\%. Beyond this the increments
continue to diminish, until we use all \(M=p=19\) components, which
captures all 100\% of the variance.

    \hypertarget{partial-least-squares}{%
\subsubsection{Partial Least Squares}\label{partial-least-squares}}

Partial least squares (PLS) is implemented in the
\texttt{PLSRegression()} function.

    \begin{tcolorbox}[breakable, size=fbox, boxrule=1pt, pad at break*=1mm,colback=cellbackground, colframe=cellborder]
\prompt{In}{incolor}{55}{\boxspacing}
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PY{n}{pls} \PY{o}{=} \PY{n}{PLSRegression}\PY{p}{(}\PY{n}{n\PYZus{}components}\PY{o}{=}\PY{l+m+mi}{2}\PY{p}{,} 
                    \PY{n}{scale}\PY{o}{=}\PY{k+kc}{True}\PY{p}{)}
\PY{n}{pls}\PY{o}{.}\PY{n}{fit}\PY{p}{(}\PY{n}{X}\PY{p}{,} \PY{n}{Y}\PY{p}{)}
\end{Verbatim}
\end{tcolorbox}

            \begin{tcolorbox}[breakable, size=fbox, boxrule=.5pt, pad at break*=1mm, opacityfill=0]
\prompt{Out}{outcolor}{55}{\boxspacing}
\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
PLSRegression()
\end{Verbatim}
\end{tcolorbox}
        
    As was the case in PCR, we will want to use CV to choose the number of
components.

    \begin{tcolorbox}[breakable, size=fbox, boxrule=1pt, pad at break*=1mm,colback=cellbackground, colframe=cellborder]
\prompt{In}{incolor}{56}{\boxspacing}
